entities.name: Buryat Academic Opera and Ballet Theater
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Buryat Academic Opera and Ballet Theater (Russian: Бурятский государственный академический театр оперы и балета, founded 1939) in Ulan-Ude, Russia — the capital of the Republic of Buryatia in Siberia near Lake Baikal — is one of the distinctive Soviet-era national opera companies that developed a fusion of European classical performing arts with the Buryat Mongolian cultural tradition, creating original operas and ballets based on Buryat epics and folk culture and providing cultural infrastructure for one of Siberia's major indigenous peoples.

The Buryat people are a Mongolic people of Siberia who maintained their distinct cultural traditions (including shamanistic practices, later mixed with Tibetan Buddhism) through centuries of Russian imperial rule. Soviet cultural policy's creation of a Buryat opera company required developing indigenous Buryat classical music — Buryat composers created operas based on the Geser Epic (the central Buryat-Mongolian heroic epic, shared with Tibetan and Mongolian traditions) and other cultural materials.

The Buryat Opera Theater's unusual cultural position — representing a Mongolian-language Buddhist people's artistic tradition in European classical form — makes it one of the most interesting examples of Soviet cultural syncretism. The theater's architecture (a distinctive Soviet Buryat-style building in Ulan-Ude) and its repertoire combining European opera and ballet with Buryat-Mongolian themes created a hybrid cultural institution that has survived the Soviet period and continues as the central performing arts institution of Buryatia.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Buryat Academic Opera and Ballet Theater — creating a unique Buryat-Mongolian classical music tradition under Soviet cultural policy, based on the Geser Epic, and continuing as the primary performing arts institution of Siberia's Buryat people — is regionally significant as one of the world's most unusual cultural syncretisms in performing arts.
